summary: Expanding two binomials applies the distributive law twice: every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second, so (x + 3)(x − 2) produces FOUR products (x², −2x, +3x, −6) that collect to x² + x − 6. It generalises the grid method for multiplying two-digit numbers — (x + 2)(x + 3) mirrors 12 × 13 as (10 + 2)(10 + 3). The grid/area model keeps all four products visible, which helps against the two most common errors: dropping the middle cross-products (writing x² − 6) and squaring each term of (a + 3)² to get a² + 9 instead of a² + 6a + 9. Directed-number care is essential for the signs; collecting like terms is a required final step.
misconceptions: Multiplies only the first terms and the last terms, MISSING the two middle cross-products, e.g. (x + 3)(x − 2) → x² − 6
Squares each term of a squared bracket: (a + 3)² → a² + 9 (or (a + b)² → a² + b²), forgetting the 2ab middle term
Sign errors with negative terms — applies a false 'same sign in the middle' rule, or drops the minus on a cross-product
Miscollects or mis-multiplies the middle/constant terms (e.g. 3b + 4b handled wrongly, or 3 × 4 written as 7)
Leaves the answer uncollected as x² + 3x − 2x − 6 instead of simplifying to x² + x − 6

activities.title: Build the expansion on a 2×2 grid
steps: Draw a 2×2 grid. Write the terms of the first bracket down the left of the rows (e.g. x and +3) and the terms of the second across the top of the columns (e.g. x and −2).
Fill each of the four cells with the product of its row term and its column term, writing the sign explicitly: x², −2x, +3x, −6. Keep a running tally of how many of the four cells you have completed.
Identify the two middle like-terms (−2x and +3x) and collect them (−2x + 3x = +x) to write the simplified answer x² + x − 6.
Connect it to numbers: set out 12 × 13 as (10 + 2)(10 + 3) on the same grid and check the four cells add to 156 (100 + 30 + 20 + 6).
activities.insight: A product of two binomials has FOUR products before collecting; the grid gives every product its own cell so none is forgotten, and it is the same idea as grid multiplication of two-digit numbers.

activities.title: Square a bracket without squaring each term
steps: Rewrite (a + 3)² as (a + 3)(a + 3) before doing anything else.
Grid it: the four cells give a², +3a, +3a, +9. Notice the two identical middle cells.
Collect the middle terms (3a + 3a = 6a) to get a² + 6a + 9.
Check numerically with a = 2: (a + 3)² = 5² = 25, while a² + 9 = 13. They disagree, so a² + 9 is wrong; a² + 6a + 9 = 4 + 12 + 9 = 25 matches.
activities.insight: Squaring a bracket means multiplying it by itself, which still produces a middle term; (a + 3)² = a² + 6a + 9, not a² + 9, and substitution confirms which form is correct.

activities.title: Link expanding to factorising and check by substitution
steps: After expanding (x + 3)(x − 2) = x² + x − 6, substitute x = 1 into both forms and confirm they match (4 × (−1) = −4; 1 + 1 − 6 = −4).
Run it backwards: given x² + x − 6, ask 'what two brackets multiply to give this?' and recover (x + 3)(x − 2).
Try a difference-of-squares case (p + 4)(p − 4): expand to p² − 16 and notice the middle terms (+4p and −4p) cancel.
activities.insight: Expanding and factorising are inverse processes; a substitution check catches errors, and some expansions (like (p+4)(p−4)) have middle terms that cancel rather than being absent.

activities.title: Fluency check with signed and squared brackets
steps: Expand and simplify (x − 2)(x + 5), showing the sign of each of the four products and the collected answer (x² + 3x − 10).
Choose the correct expansion of (a + 3)² from several options, one of which is the common wrong answer a² + 9, and explain why that answer is wrong.
Fill in the missing middle terms of a partly-completed grid for a given bracket pair, then collect.
activities.insight: Fluency means producing all four correctly-signed products and collecting them, and recognising the signature wrong answers (x² − 6 for a missing middle, a² + 9 for term-by-term squaring).

checkQuestion: Expand and simplify these two, showing all your working. First: (x + 3)(x − 2). Then: (a + 3)². Say nothing about which method to use — just work them out.
checkAnswer: (x + 3)(x − 2) = x² + x − 6 (from the four products x², −2x, +3x, −6, collecting −2x + 3x = +x). (a + 3)² = a² + 6a + 9 (because it means (a + 3)(a + 3); the middle terms 3a + 3a give 6a).
